### Observed differences

- Resource allocation changed across six activities. In the earlier window, assignments of A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 were dominated by one stable group of resources, with the largest individual shares around 10–11% (led by User_18) and several further resources at roughly 4–9%. In the later window, two resources that played no visible role before — User_35 (about 9–11% of assignments) and User_15 (about 8–9%) — head every list, while the earlier leaders fall to about 4–6% or drop out of the top lists; in one activity the former top resource fell from about 12% to about 6%. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- The shift is consistent in size and direction: dissimilarity of about 0.33–0.38 in all six activities, each difference larger than in about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits. The combined share of the ten largest resources barely moves (the residual bucket goes from about 33–47% to about 34–47%), so work was reshuffled between groups of resources rather than concentrated or reduced. The profiles rest on roughly 100–260 assignments per window (fewest for A22: 106 before, 128 after). [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A13 and A14 show exactly identical resource profiles in both windows, so they most likely mirror one underlying behaviour rather than two independent changes. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- Timing: the elapsed time between consecutive completion events of A04 and A01 decreased — mean from about 48 to about 24 hours, median from about 33 to about 25 hours. The fastest quarter of gaps is nearly unchanged (about 0.1 hours in both windows), while the 75th percentile fell from about 46 to 35 hours and the spread halved (standard deviation about 71 to 31 hours), so the reduction comes mainly from the longest gaps shortening. The item covers all 200 traces in each window. [TWAIT001]
- Screening context: no control-flow unit qualified (0 of 32, against about 0.16 expected by chance); one time unit and all six resource units qualified, against about 0.017 and 0.003 expected respectively. [TWAIT001, ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a change in resource allocation: in the later window, the work on six activities — A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 — is assigned to a largely different group of resources than before. Earlier, one stable group led every activity (top individual shares about 6–12%, led by User_18); later, User_35 and User_15 — absent from the earlier top lists — hold the largest shares (about 9–11% and 8–9%), while the previous leaders shrink to about 4–6% or leave the top lists. The hypothesis is direct (the indicator measures allocation itself), consistent (the same direction in all six activities, each beyond about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits), and the resource family produced six qualifying items where about 0.003 were expected without change, with no qualifying control-flow item — so the difference is in who executes the work, not in structure at these thresholds. Limitations: the identifiers are anonymous codes, so nothing can be said about what the groups represent; A13 and A14 share identical profiles and are not independent confirmations; and a change in the mix of cases reaching these activities (different case types routed to different resource pools) could produce the same pattern — the evidence cannot separate a reallocation from such a case-mix change. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Other differences: The elapsed time between consecutive completions of A04 and A01 decreased (mean about 48 to 24 hours, median about 33 to 25 hours, with the longest gaps shortening most). This is a timing difference in its own right; it rests on a single item (1 against about 0.017 expected by chance in the time family), so on its own it sits at the edge of what an unchanged process produces, and any connection to the reallocation cannot be established from this evidence. [TWAIT001]
